children: U.S. and European wheat futures tumbled on Thursday, retreating from multi-year highs, after Russian President Vladimir Putin said there was a chance of a peace agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

Traders said Putin's remarks triggered profit-taking after a steep rally in the past month linked to mounting concerns about the war disrupting crucial Black Sea grain exports from Russia and Ukraine.
The most traded wheat contract
on the Chicago Board of Trade was down 3.6% at $7.46-1/4 a bushel by 1106 GMT.
The benchmark hit its highest since February 2023 on Wednesday at $7.95, building on a 21% monthly rise in August.
On Euronext, December wheat
was down 4.7% at €244.75 a metric ton, pulling back from Wednesday's contract high of €259.25, which also marked a two-year peak for a second-month price
"The Black Sea situation is responsible for 80/90% of the wheat rally last month, so any chance of peace means profit-taking," a European trader said.

Putin told an economic forum in Russia's Far East there was a chance of a peace agreement in Ukraine, but restarting talks was harder because of Ukrainian attacks on shipping and a call by Kyiv for civilian aircraft to avoid Russian airspace.
Some traders cautioned that Putin's remarks did not suggest an immediate prospect of military de-escalation and that physical disruption to Black Sea grain flows was unchanged.
"Funds are very long so I can see a retracement happening, but not prices collapsing," another European trader said. "The problem is still logistics and how to get all the grain out."
Ukraine's combined grain and oilseed exports fell to 1.2 million metric tons in August from 2.5 million tons in July, Ukrainian traders union UGA said on Thursday.
Traders are watching to see how suppliers will approach a wheat import tender announced on Thursday by Saudi Arabia, for which Russia is a regular supplier.
Corn and soybean prices tracked the weakness in wheat.
CBOT corn
dropped 2.3% to $5.31-1/4 a bushel after hitting a three-year high on Wednesday, while soybeans
fell 0.9% to $12.99 following a 2-1/2-year high in the previous session.
The corn market has been supported since last month by falling expectations for U.S. harvest yields, while soybeans have been boosted by a run of Chinese purchases.
The market will get an update on overseas demand later on Thursday from weekly U.S. grain export sales figures.
